title: Disaster Recovery Planning
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Disaster Recovery Planning.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to defining recovery objectives.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Disaster Recovery Planning. Its primary job is to help you set recovery objectives, choose an appropriate backup type, restore into isolation and verify recoverability. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing disaster recovery planning teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: set recovery objectives, choose an appropriate backup type, restore into isolation and verify recoverability. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

items.title: Defining recovery objectives
items.text: Write down the recovery objective and confirm it by restoring into an isolated target; a successful dump alone is not a restore test.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Disaster Recovery Planning
content_blocks.expected_output: Creates a custom-format logical dump if credentials, connectivity and privileges are valid.
content_blocks.safety_note: Backups may contain private data. Keep them encrypted and do not place real credentials or dumps in the course ZIP.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a local lab database and a connection variable configured outside shared files. Restore into a separate target and verify it.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

Treat the sample as inspectable code unless you run it yourself in an approved isolated environment. Python examples require a separate isolated runner.
content_blocks.schema_assumptions: Use a local lab database and a connection variable configured outside shared files. Restore into a separate target and verify it.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: A backup has value only when restore is rehearsed and verified. Keep backup artifacts protected, restore to a separate target, and record the recovery point and limitations.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Disaster Recovery Planning”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Defining recovery objectives”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Defining recovery objectives”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Disaster Recovery Planning, with an explanation of “Defining recovery objectives”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Disaster Recovery Planning fits into the broader goal to set recovery objectives, choose an appropriate backup type, restore into isolation and verify recoverability.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Defining recovery objectives, Backup failure scenarios, Data-loss and corruption scenarios.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
